about:
The cases of acceptModelSources(raw, hosts) in src/tools/modelManifest.ts, which decides the extra places a remote answer may name for fetching the speech model. Two readers must give exactly these answers: the TypeScript test (src/tools/modelManifest.test.ts, which also checks that max_sources, max_length and allowed_hosts are the function's own, that every accept_entry is written the way the parser writes it, and that an answer holds only entries that were in the list it was given) and the server's Python twin.

THE RULES. The answer is a list of strings, worked out like this:
1. raw must be a list (a JSON array). Anything else (null, a string, an object, a number, true) gives [].
2. The list may hold at most max_sources entries, counted BEFORE repeats are removed. More gives [].
3. EVERY entry must be acceptable (rules 4 to 11). If one is not, the answer is [] (a list is never trusted in part).
4. An acceptable entry is a string. A number, null, true, an object or a nested list is not.
5. It is at most max_length characters long, counted as JavaScript counts them (UTF-16 code units, the string as given). Rule 11 leaves only ASCII strings, so for any string that can pass, UTF-16 code units, code points and bytes are the same count.
6. It is an https address: the scheme is https (not http, ftp, wss, file, data or javascript; an address with no scheme is refused too).
7. It has no user-info (nothing like name@ or name:password@ before the host), no port (not 8443, and not even 443 or an empty port after a colon) and no fragment (no # anywhere, not even a bare # at the end; %23 is just an escape and is fine).
8. Its host (for a string that passes rule 11, the text between https:// and the next slash) is a public name: at least two labels (the parts between dots), none of them empty (no leading dot, no trailing dot, no two dots in a row), every label made only of the lower-case letters a to z, digits and hyphens, not starting or ending with a hyphen and not starting with xn-- (no internationalised names), the last label not made only of digits (that is an IPv4 address in disguise), not localhost and not a name under localhost, and not an IPv6 address in brackets.
9. The host is one of allowed_hosts or a name under one (it ends with a dot and then that name). allowed_hosts are lower case.
10. Nothing else about the path or the query is limited: a query is allowed (an empty one too), and capitals, dots, dashes, underscores, at signs and escapes in them are fine.
11. CANONICAL: the string is already written exactly the way the WHATWG URL parser writes it. In JavaScript: new URL(entry).href === entry. An address that needed any cleaning up is refused, never repaired, so that no other program has to reproduce the parser to agree with this one.
12. The entries that pass come back exactly as given, in the order given, each once: an entry equal character for character to an earlier one is dropped and the first is kept. Two entries that differ only in the capitals of their path are two places.

CANONICAL FORM, in plain words. The string is ASCII only: printable characters from ! to ~, so no space, no control character, no tab or newline (not even at the ends) and nothing outside ASCII. The scheme and the host are in lower case (capitals in the path and the query are kept by the parser and are fine). The host is written the way the parser writes it: a letter outside ASCII, a full-width letter, an ideographic full stop, a soft hyphen or a zero-width space in a host is rewritten or dropped by the parser, so it is not canonical. There is no default port (no :443, no empty port). There is a path and it starts with a slash: https://huggingface.co is not canonical, https://huggingface.co/ is, and so is a slash followed by a query. There are no dot segments: no path segment that is . or .., and a dot written as the escape %2e (in either letter case) counts as a dot, so %2e, .%2E, %2e. and %2E%2e are dot segments too; a segment such as ... or b..c or .d is fine. Only forward slashes: a backslash is rewritten to a slash. Every character the parser would percent-encode is written as an escape with UPPER-case hex digits: a space is %20, a letter outside ASCII is its UTF-8 bytes (%C3%A9), and the same goes for control characters, DEL and, in the path, the characters double quote, less-than, greater-than, left brace, right brace and backtick, and, in the query, double quote, less-than, greater-than and the apostrophe. An escape that is ALREADY in the string is left alone by the parser whatever its hex digits (%2f, %2F and %c3%a9 are all canonical, and they are different strings), so is an escape of a plain letter (%41), and so is a % that starts no escape. A reader that has no URL parser decides rule 11 with a pattern, and must never accept a string that is not canonical. Where the parser's behaviour is exotic and no case in this file shows it (for example the other ASCII characters the parser keeps in a path, such as ^ or |), a reader that cannot be sure must refuse: refusing a place the function would take is harmless, taking one it refuses is not.

HOW A READER USES THE DATA, with hosts = allowed_hosts: legit_entry is itself accepted; for each refuse_entry, accept([entry]), accept([legit_entry, entry]) and accept([entry, legit_entry]) are all []; for each accept_entry, accept([entry]) == [entry] (it is already canonical, so nothing is rewritten); for each lists case, accept(raw) == expect, where raw is any JSON value (null, a string, an object, a number, nested lists, a list).
